title: Measuring Authorization Drift Across Relational, NoSQL and Vector Stores: A Leak-Window Metric and a Paired Comparison of Outbox and Ledger-Anchored Revocation
content: When one record lives in relational, document and vector stores, revoking a principal is only as strong as the slowest store. We define the Leak Window—from the revoke to the last instant the record remains retrievable through any layer—measured by a poller that queries the stores directly and never consults the system under test. Four architectures are compared: an uncoordinated polyglot stack, a transactional outbox, a converged PostgreSQL instance with pgvector and row-level security, and a ledger-anchored revocation bridge. Consolidation does not help: four of six read paths through one database still serve revoked data, and a pooled connection inheriting a stale session variable leaked on 150 of 150 calls. The uncoordinated stack closes within tens of milliseconds when nothing fails, but leaks without bound and in silence when store writes are dropped (35 of 49 valid trials at 10,000 records, p = 0.30); the bridge’s healthy-path window is 2.67 s. A paired ablation shows what each mechanism buys: concurrency shortens the window but not the loss rate, bounded retry recovers 44 of 50 trials and the outbox’s unbounded retry 50 of 50, an append-only table makes the outcome answerable, and the ledger adds only an audit record the tested administrator could not alter, for 5.1 s more. No false containment was observed, and the window is unchanged by a hundredfold more data.
